title: The root span a generation exports, in three languages
pins: The name, status and attribute map of the ROOT span one generation exports. A span is read by a backend that does not know which language produced it: Phoenix groups by `session.id`, filters by `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` and `gen_ai.operation.name`, and dedupes on `input.value`. Every one of those is a string comparison against spans from other services, so a key or a value spelled differently in one language does not error — the two services simply stop appearing in the same result, and a dashboard that looks complete is quietly missing half its traffic. The security half is narrower and sharper: `input.value` carries user content, and a span leaves the application. Since 2026-09-05 it also pins the PROVIDER RATE LIMITS the bridge exports — `prism.rate_limit.*`, which is a custom namespace because the GenAI conventions define nothing for quota (see `findings`). Those rows carry the suite's only adversarial INPUT that is not content: a bucket name is chosen by the provider and becomes part of an attribute KEY, which is the G-36 shape one layer out. The rate-limit rows are handed to every language as the completion event's own argument; before 2026-09-05 the reference could only be given them inside a response, which is G-45.
scope: The root span only. Step and tool spans are a separate value with a separate failure mode and are NOT covered here. Neither is the FAILED root span: the bridges also export rate limits off a rate-limited exception, in all three languages, and that path is asserted in each package's own suite rather than here. This suite existing does not make the opentelemetry family conformance-verified.
construction: Each case supplies the generation in Prism's own neutral vocabulary — a `TelemetryOperation` value (text, structured, embeddings, image, stream) and a `FinishReason` value (stop, tool-calls) — and lets every language map it as it does. No language is handed a value pre-translated into its own spelling, which would hide the mapping being compared. That the ports EXPECT this vocabulary is not an assumption: their own root-kind branch tests for `text` and `structured` by name.
findings:
ZERO of the first thirteen rows agree across all three languages, in six distinct classes. Registered as G-23 through G-28 in .ai/plans/port-gaps-register.md; each is pinned in the negative in the three runners, so whoever fixes one gets a red test that forces the corpus to be regenerated in the same change. Summarised because a reader who sees `agrees: false` on every row learns nothing about which of six problems they are looking at: (1) `gen_ai.operation.name` and the span name — the reference maps onto the GenAI convention's own vocabulary, the ports pass Prism's internal operation string straight through; (2) `openinference.span.kind` for image and stream; (3) span status on success — the reference leaves it unset, the ports set ok; (4) `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` — the reference emits the PHP enum's CASE NAME, the ports the neutral value; (5) the JSON encoding of captured content — Python's dumps defaults put a space after every separator and escape non-ASCII; (6) the truncation ruler — bytes, UTF-16 code units and escaped characters give three different strings from one input, none of which errors.

RATE LIMITS (otel-0014..0018, added 2026-09-05) are the first thing in this suite that AGREES: all 48 `prism.rate_limit.*` attributes are byte-identical in all three languages, and the five rows still carry `agrees: false` only because of the four pre-existing classes above. Two decisions are recorded here because they are observable and were made rather than inherited. FIRST, THERE IS NO STANDARD. The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define no attribute for rate limits or quota — checked 2026-09-05 against the gen_ai and http attribute registries; `gen_ai.*` has usage, request and response namespaces and no quota in any of them, `gen_ai.error.type` has a `rate_limit` member that names a failure rather than a headroom, and the closest mechanism anywhere in semconv is the generic opt-in `http.response.header.<key>` capture, which records a header verbatim and knows nothing about which bucket it describes. So the names are custom, and they sit under `prism.` rather than inside `gen_ai.` precisely BECAUSE there is no standard yet: squatting in a reserved namespace is worse than being outside it, since a real `gen_ai.rate_limit.*` must be free to arrive later without two spellings meaning subtly different things. SECOND, THE LIST IS FLATTENED BY BUCKET NAME — `prism.rate_limit.tokens.remaining`, not `...0.remaining` and not one serialised JSON blob — because a backend has to be able to FILTER on it, which a blob forbids and an index makes depend on the order the provider happened to answer in. The cost is that the attribute KEY SPACE becomes provider-controlled, so a name is accepted only if every character is in an explicit ASCII set spelled identically in the three languages, at most 16 buckets reach a span, and a duplicate name loses to the first. otel-0017 is the row that matters: it feeds seven hostile spellings of `tokens` — trailing space, trailing newline, case fold, Cyrillic homoglyph, an embedded dot that would forge a nested key, an empty name, and a duplicate appended after the real bucket — and all three languages drop every one and keep the real bucket's numbers. The reset instant is an INTEGER Unix epoch in seconds (`resets_at_unix`) and never a formatted date, because a date is where three languages produce three strings from one instant. otel-0016 pins the other half of `only export what exists`: an empty bucket list writes no attribute at all rather than an empty array, which matters because an empty list is the COMMON case — most reference providers report none, and so does every span a stream produces, in all three languages, because core's streaming events carry no Meta.

THIRD, ADDED WHEN G-45 CLOSED ON 2026-09-05: all three runners now hand the buckets to the bridge THE SAME WAY, as the completion event's own argument beside usage. They did not before. The reference's only channel was the response's Meta, and core nulls the response when `prism.telemetry.capture_content` is off — the default — so a case declaring quota had to hand PHP a response object in a state core never produces. These five rows therefore agreed byte for byte while a real successful generation exported NO rate limits at all. Not one recorded span changed when it was fixed, and that is the part worth keeping: a corpus compares OUTPUTS, so a defect that lives entirely in how the input reaches the code is invisible to it by construction — the same shape as a bug all three languages share. The asymmetry in the construction was the only tell, which is why it was written down. It is pinned now where it is reachable rather than here: `prism-opentelemetry:tests/Feature/ContentGateTest.php` drives core's telemetry layer and the bridge together with the content gate shut, and goes red if the buckets are put back behind it.
